ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 7 — Preventive Visit — Nikola Tesla

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

text.paragraph: Periodic preventive visit; no new complaints. [S]

Mr. Tesla is a 46-year-old electrical engineer with obsessive-compulsive disorder who comes for his periodic preventive visit. He completed the health risk assessment before the visit. The gastroenteritis in August settled within three days; he restarted sertraline the next morning, and the nurse telephone check found him drinking well. The flare in washing lasted about a week and his therapist used it as exposure practice. He takes sertraline 150 mg every morning, has finished the course of exposure and response prevention, and sees the therapist monthly. Today's Y-BOCS is 12. He eats three meals a day, sleeps about six hours, and walks most days. He has had no suicidal thoughts. [S]

Obsessive-compulsive disorder, severe (Y-BOCS 28), with good insight: contamination, symmetry, and number obsessions; washing, counting, repeating in threes, and calculating compulsions; synthetic modern diagnosis linked to his own accounts of counting and calculating rituals and aversions

S — Synthetic modern diagnosis. His rituals and aversions are documented in his own words (D); calling them obsessive-compulsive disorder is a retrospective interpretation (R), and no diagnosis was made in his lifetime.
Irritant contact dermatitis of both hands from washing them 40 to 60 times a day
S — Synthetic consequence of washing compulsions.

S — Synthetic nutritional consequence echoing his documented habit of calculating the volume of food before eating.
Insufficient sleep, four hours a night, from late work and night-time rituals
S — Synthetic sleep problem echoing his documented claims about very short sleep.
Acute viral gastroenteritis, probably norovirus, with mild dehydration; resolved

S — Synthetic acute illness at an unscheduled visit, chosen to teach rehydration, sertraline during vomiting, antiemetic interactions, and infection-control advice that does not feed contamination rituals; it does not echo any documented illness.

Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 20 minutes, with his consent. He named a health care agent, the longest-serving engineer on his staff, and completed a health care proxy form; the agent is recorded in the chart and is not named here. He said that what matters most to him is being able to think clearly and to keep working on his inventions. He wants full treatment for reversible illness. He asked that any clinician caring for him in hospital be told about his OCD so that hygiene routines can be explained to him rather than imposed, and he agreed to keep his safety plan with his proxy form. He chose not to record other specific treatment preferences today. The plan will be revisited yearly. [S]
